newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Who will buy the 2-yr notes?.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Who will buy the 2-yr notes?.

text.p: With no economic news scheduled, the U.S. Treasury market turns its focus to new supply Wednesday and players wonder where the buying is going to come from.
"In the past few days, we have not seen any foreign buyers," said Richard Schwarz, a trader at Zions First National Bank.
The Treasury is slated to sell $18.25 billion two-year notes Wednesday afternoon, followed by another $12.5 billion five-year notes Thursday.

The when-issued two-year note was trading at 5.85 percent late Tuesday. Traders said that it is unlikely the supply can be successfully taken down at that level. Some suggested a level of closer to 5.90 percent of above.
"The Street would like the market to be weak heading into the auction," said a trader at a New York-based primary dealership.
Schwarz said the note could go as high as six percent, which would be 25 basis points higher from where it was announced last week.
"The Street doesn't want to take anything down at these prices," he said. "The market is artificially high where Federal funds are and where they are perceived to be.
"If foreign buying comes in, it will turn the market around. If not, we will keep going lower."

He said that much still depends on the Federal Reserve. The Fed left rates steady at its policy setting meeting Tuesday, which means it is highly probable rates will remain where they are until its next meeting in early February.
Meanwhile, traders said there are no flows to speak of -- just choppy trading.
One trader noted that part of the market's problem in the past couple weeks has been heavy corporate supply issuance.
"People hedging Treasuries for corporates and less pronounced foreign buying" has weighed on the market, he said.
Some said they anticipated a boost to the market the next couple days, when maturing cash management bills are seen being reinvensted to the short end -- two-years and in.
As such, traders see the latest selloff as merely a correction and not the start of a bear market, despite it wiping out all of the gains made in November.
After the supply is gone, players said they will look at the strength of holiday shopping.
"The concern is, if we have a good Christmas season the Fed may think about tightening and we will have some backing up to do," Schwarz said.

"So, the next phase is we have to think what the Fed might be doing come February. Until February, if there is no retail interest -- foreign and domestic-based -- we will most likely continue to back up to levels where it brings retail in."

Late Tuesday, the 30-year bond was at 97-29/32, down 14/32, to yield 6.66 percent. The 10-year note was 11/32 lower at 100-18/32 and yielding 6.42 percent, while the two-year was at 99-18/32, down 3/32, to yield 5.86 percent. The three-month bill was up seven basis points at 4.89 percent.
